title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest
claim: A randomized recursive partitioning process can be modeled as a random walk over interval states that ends at an absorbing state.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels with 1-D axes; staircase trajectory arrows; shared legend top-right
description: Two side-by-side panels show example random-walk trajectories for isolation trees. Each panel has a 2-D coordinate system with left index ℓ on the horizontal axis and right index r on the vertical axis. Both are labeled x1 to x7. A solid diagonal line runs from x1 at the top-left to x7 at the bottom-right. Dashed grid lines mark candidate split positions. A black initial point sits at the origin. Blue intermediate points and a red absorbing point sit on the diagonal near x4. Dark arrows trace a staircase path between them. A 1-D number line with black, blue and red dots and brackets sits beside the vertical axis and below the horizontal axis of each panel. The brackets show the current interval as it shrinks. A boxed legend at top right explains the colors: black is the initial state, blue is intermediate, red is absorbing, and an arrow is the trajectory. The eye goes first to the staircase arrows and the red absorbing point.
caption: Examples of the random walk model for iTrees. The points colored in black, blue, and red indicate the initial, intermediate, and absorbing states, respectively. The lines with arrows indicate the trajectory of the transition process.
abstract: Isolation Forest (iForest) stands out as a widely-used unsupervised anomaly detector, primarily owing to its remarkable runtime efficiency and superior performance in large-scale tasks. Despite its widespread adoption, a theoretical foundation explaining iForest's success remains unclear. This paper focuses on the inductive bias of iForest, which theoretically elucidates under what circumstances and to what extent iForest works well. The key is to formulate the growth process of iForest, where the split dimensions and split values are randomly selected. We model the growth process of iForest as a random walk, enabling us to derive the expected depth function, which is the outcome of iForest, using transition probabilities. The case studies reveal key inductive biases: iForest exhibits lower sensitivity to central anomalies while demonstrating greater parameter adaptability compared to $k$-Nearest Neighbor. Our study provides a theoretical understanding of the effectiveness of iForest and establishes a foundation for further theoretical exploration.
